summary:
Our project is an interactive online atlas that brings 11 different Earth models together in one place. Each model simulates a distinct environment in detail, including the Shackleton Ridge on the Moon and three key regions of Mars: Meridiani Plain, Medusa Trough, and Deuterium Uplift. To ground these simulations in real data, we combined NASA's super-Earth datasets with years of climate records from ERA5, and added fault-location markers for every model.

The atlas directly addresses the challenge by turning scattered planetary and climate data into a single, accessible tool that anyone can explore and compare. Users can work with any number of instruments, rovers, and extraction technologies inside a consistent abstract framework, which makes it possible to estimate the physical limits and biases of each model with reasonable accuracy.

This matters because reliable, comparable models are essential for planning exploration and resource use beyond Earth. By making those models interactive and transparent, our atlas helps researchers, students, and mission planners make better-informed decisions.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Earth analogs for the Moon and Mars is a public, interactive website that helps engineers and scientists decide where on Earth to test hardware, instruments, and operations for four off-world targets: the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge at the lunar south pole, and three Mars regions, Meridiani Planum, the Medusae Fossae Formation, and Deuteronilus Mensae. It presents eleven Earth field stations on an interactive map, each with its own page. Every page states why the site is an analog, which specific test it supports (for example Raman and near-infrared spectrometer calibration on sulfate crusts, landing-algorithm and rover-traction tests on an evaporite plain, UAV obstacle avoidance among yardangs, or drilling into an ice-rich rock-glacier core), how that test would advance research, the measured climate at the site, and an explicit section on where the analogy breaks.

The project has two stages. First, a research pipeline screened 45 candidate sites through six rounds (discovery, screening, data collection, adversarial verification, diversification, and freeze), followed by a novelty rebalance. It applied hard filters (a point site, at least two documented extreme attributes, obtainable public data, legal access, and no duplicate within 100 km) and a scored set of soft preferences. Every number was tied to a registered source with its URL, access date, and a verbatim quote, and values that could not be retrieved were recorded as “NOT FOUND” instead of being filled in. Second, a build stage generates the public site: Python scripts download NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily air temperature for 2015–2024 (3,653 days per site) plus 2001–2025 humidity and wind climatology, and ERA5 precipitation. They compute hot-month maximum, cold-month minimum, daily range, annual mean, seasonal amplitude, humidity, wind, and precipitation, adjust temperatures from the coarse grid-cell elevation to each site’s elevation (6.5 °C/km), and generate the static pages.

What benefits does it have?

Field testing on Earth is cheaper and faster than testing in space, but only if the test site fits the test. Our pages let a planner see what each site can and cannot do. Every value is traceable to a raw data file, and values taken from the project reports (mineralogy, porosity, ice content, slopes) are labelled as reported claims rather than measurements, because the reports give no per-number citations.

What is the intended impact?

To reduce the risk and cost of preparing lunar and Martian missions by matching each test to a suitable Earth site, and to widen the set of sites considered. We deliberately included lesser-known sites, such as Campo de Piedra Pómez, Tuz Gölü, Valea Rea in the Retezat Mountains, and Aktash rock glacier. Where a site is close to a heavily studied analog region, its page says so.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Python 3 for data retrieval, processing, and page generation. HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript for the site, with Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map, Esri basemap tiles, and the Archivo and Source Serif 4 fonts. Data came from NASA POWER (MERRA-2), ERA5 (via the Open-Meteo archive), MODIS land-surface temperature (MOD11A2, via ORNL DAAC), Copernicus DEM 30 m, SRTM, ArcticDEM and REMA elevation models, the Australian SILO climate dataset, the LRO LOLA lunar elevation model (from the NASA PDS Geosciences Node), and the OpenAlex literature index. No special hardware was used.

How is your project creative?

Instead of claiming that a site “looks like Mars,” each station is tied to one specific test and to a stated limit. The project is also open about its own weaknesses. Our data show that two-metre air temperature barely separates the eleven sites (mean daily ranges all fall between 5 and 18 °C), so the site says this directly and names land-surface temperature from MODIS or ECOSTRESS as the next step. Our research stage also audited itself against the challenge’s own advice to look beyond famous analogs: it replaced four well-known sites (including an Atacama site, an Iceland site, and Craters of the Moon), cutting the share of sites in the four named heavily studied regions from 4 of 10 to 2 of 10, while keeping a deliberate mix of recognised anchors and less-used sites. The map has light and dark themes, works with a plain station list if JavaScript is unavailable, and includes keyboard and reduced-motion support.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Novelty: we checked whether tests of the kind we propose had already been carried out at the analog site we found, and we favoured tests that would add something new. Each station page has a “How it advances research” section for this reason.
  • Partial analogs: a site can match geology but not terrain. For example, Corta Atalaya reproduces Meridiani’s jarosite–hematite mineralogy, but its 38–45° quarry walls contradict Meridiani’s sub-1° plain, and its ~980 mbar pressure is nothing like ~6.1 mbar. The page says this openly.
  • Data quality: MERRA-2 precipitation is unreliable at high-altitude arid cells (563 mm/yr versus 79 mm/yr from ERA5 at Campo de Piedra Pómez), so we used ERA5 for precipitation.
  • Elevation mismatch between grid cells and sites, handled with a documented lapse-rate correction.
  • Scale: the research stage computed terrain metrics at both 20 km and 1 km, because a small area can match better than a whole region.
  • Earth’s limits: gravity, atmospheric pressure, vacuum, and radiation cannot be reproduced on Earth.
  • Access and ethics: sites had to be legally visitable, and we scored biosensitivity so as not to propose tests in strictly protected areas.
  • Transparency and reproducibility: nothing is estimated or interpolated, missing values are omitted, and the site can be rebuilt with two commands.
